Hollis Fen is not much to look at in August: a shallow bowl of peat and sedge in the coastal hills, drying at the edges. It is, however, the only place where the banded fen salamander has been counted the same way for fifty years. Emeka Okonjo walked its transects in 1974 with a headlamp and a notebook, and reported a single continuous population spread evenly across the basin, noting in his summary that no corner of the fen held more animals than any other.

Naomi Farrar inherited the transects in 2011. She kept Okonjo's routes and his hours and added a grid of pit tags — rice-sized chips, read by an antenna on a pole, that register an animal without anyone having to hold it. For eight seasons the counts behaved. Then the summer of 2019 took nine weeks of rain out of the fen.

Farrar expected the drought to show up as an absence. What the antennas gave her instead was a crowd. Of two hundred forty tagged animals, two hundred twelve were read within forty meters of three cold seeps on the north rim. Distance from water had become the check on where a salamander could go.

The obvious objection is that tags are not animals: a chip that goes unread may mean a salamander that moved, or an antenna that failed. Farrar spent two seasons on that objection, walking a second grid by hand each week to see whether the machines and her eyes agreed. They did, within eleven percent.

Farrar is careful about Okonjo. He counted what was there to count, she says, and in a wet decade the seeps are simply not where the animals are. What the drought exposed was not an error but a structure: a fen that becomes, in a dry year, three small places.

Fifty years is a long time to keep a route. The fen is smaller than it was, and Farrar's grid now reaches ground Okonjo recorded as open water. She counts it anyway, and files the sheets in his old green boxes.

Devlin, the other apprentice, who had arrived a season ahead of me, told me not to ask what any of it was for. I asked anyway, in February, when my patience gave out.

On the gravel flats of the Karoo, the mottled nightjar builds nothing at all. The female scrapes a shallow hollow in the open ground, lays two eggs the colour of lichen, and settles over them so still that a hiker can pass within a metre and never look down. The arrangement works: in four seasons of watching, fewer than one nest in ten was found by a fox or a crow. Which is what makes the birds' other habit so hard to explain. In roughly a third of nests the pair simply walks away. The eggs are intact; the two birds scrape a fresh hollow somewhere else and begin again.

Mira Osei spent those four seasons near Loxton, on her knees with a notebook, counting hollows. The departures were not scattered evenly. They tracked how long a hollow had already been in use: hollows occupied more than nine days accounted for four of every five abandonments, while a hollow scraped within the past week was almost never left. The pattern held in wet years and dry ones alike.

The obvious suspect was predation — a fox passing close enough to unsettle a pair without ever finding the clutch. Osei tested the idea by moving eggs between hollows. Eggs carried into a hollow that had been in use for nine days were abandoned within three days, whatever pair had laid them. The same eggs' parents, given a hollow scraped that morning, sat tight to hatching. The trigger travelled with the hollow's age, not with the clutch or with the birds.

The pairs that left did not go far; the new hollow averaged forty metres from the old, and no pair returned to a hollow from an earlier year. Osei sieved sand from both. A hollow in long use held as many as three hundred nest mites in a handful; a fresh one held almost none. Walking away, she argues, is a check on the mites — the only one a bird that carries no nest with it can apply.

None of this makes the nightjar a planner. The bird holds no model of the season in its head; it holds a rule, and the rule was shaped by what the flats did to birds that lacked it. What the case offers is a reminder that behaviour which looks like waste from the outside may be the cheapest line in the animal's budget — and that the way to find out is to count, for four seasons, the things nobody thought worth counting.

On the gravel flats of the Karoo, the mottled nightjar builds nothing at all. The female scrapes a shallow hollow in the open ground, lays two eggs the colour of lichen, and settles over them so still that a hiker can pass within a metre and never look down. The arrangement works: in four seasons of watching, fewer than one nest in ten was found by a fox or a crow. Which is what makes the birds' other habit so hard to explain. In roughly a third of nests the pair simply walks away. The eggs are intact; the two birds scrape a fresh hollow somewhere else and begin again.

Mira Osei spent those four seasons near Loxton, on her knees with a notebook, counting hollows. The departures were not scattered evenly. They tracked the lie of the land: hollows set in the shallow drainage channels accounted for four of every five abandonments, though such hollows were only a quarter of the total. The pattern held in the first season and the fourth alike.

The obvious suspect was predation — a fox passing close enough to unsettle a pair without ever finding the clutch. Osei tested the idea by moving eggs between hollows. Eggs carried into a channel hollow were abandoned within three days even in a rainless week, whatever pair had laid them. The same eggs' parents, given a hollow on the rise between channels, sat through a downpour. The trigger travelled with the shape of the ground, not with the clutch or with the birds.

The pairs that left did not go far; the new hollow averaged forty metres away, always onto the low rise between two channels. Osei mapped every hollow she found. In January the channels ran ankle-deep for an hour after each storm, and drowned clutches lay in them; the rise stayed dry. On her map every abandoned hollow carries a check in red, and the checks fall in lines along the channels.
